Chapter 3. Why Equality Makes Societies Healthier and Happier
You know, it’s easy to believe that more money always means a better life. I mean, who wouldn’t want a bigger paycheck or a fancier place to live, right?
But life’s not that simple. Once you’ve got your basic needs covered, what really sets a good life apart from a tough one isn’t just how much money you have—it’s how that money is spread out in your community.
Think about countries where the gap between rich and poor isn’t so wide. People there usually live longer, healthier lives. But why is that? It’s not just about having access to doctors or hospitals.
It’s about how people feel every day—valued, respected, included. When you’re not worried about being left out or looked down on, your stress drops. Your body actually responds, and your health improves.
Picture a group of kids growing up where most families make about the same. They go to the same schools, play in the same parks, and dream about similar futures. There’s no big pressure to show off or to hide what you don’t have.
Friendships come easier. Bullying doesn’t have as much room to grow. That strong sense of belonging? It sticks with them, even as adults.
Now, let’s flip that. In places where the gap is huge, kids notice. Who’s wearing the newest sneakers? Who brings lunch from home—and who doesn’t? Who gets picked up in a shiny new car?
These little things add up. They shape how kids see themselves and what they think is possible. Some pull back, others act out. And that feeling of being “less than” can stick around for years, casting a shadow over health and happiness.
And it’s not just kids. Adults feel it too. In more equal societies, people trust each other more and feel better about life. They feel safer, more connected to their neighbors, and look ahead with more optimism.
There’s a real sense of “us,” not just “me versus them.” And this isn’t just hope talking—we see it in data from all over the world.
When it comes to mental health, equality matters a lot. Places where the gap is smaller see lower rates of depression and anxiety. People don’t feel as much pressure to constantly prove themselves, and there’s less shame in asking for help.
The social safety net is stronger, so folks know they won’t be left to struggle alone.
Even physical health gets a boost. People live longer, and chronic illness isn’t as common. Sure, it’s complicated, but a lot of it comes down to stress. When you feel safe and valued, your body’s just better at fighting off sickness and bouncing back from tough times.
And here’s something interesting—it’s not only the poor who benefit. Even folks at the top do better in more equal societies. There’s less cutthroat competition, and people are more willing to help each other out. The whole community gets stronger and can handle tough times together.
So, here’s the real takeaway: equality isn’t just about doing the right thing. It’s a smart move for everyone. When we close the gap between rich and poor, everybody wins. Health improves, people are happier, and the bonds between us all get even stronger.
